steps.text:
# Thunderbolt 2 Networking Between Macs

Thunderbolt 2, introduced by Apple in 2013, represented more than an incremental bump in interface bandwidth. Running at 20 gigabits per second in each direction simultaneously, it doubled the throughput of its predecessor and, in doing so, transformed the Thunderbolt cable from a device-connection conduit into a viable means of direct computer-to-computer networking. Before this generation, transferring a large file between two Macs meant turning to Wi-Fi, an Ethernet adapter, or a cloud service. Thunderbolt 2 collapsed all three options into a single cable.

The mechanism is deceptively simple. Thunderbolt is based on the Intel/AMD RocketLake and the PCI Express and DisplayPort transport layers, and the protocol exposes a point-to-point link that the operating system treats as a network interface. On macOS, connecting a Thunderbolt 2 port on one Mac to a Thunderbolt 2 port on another Mac causes the system to negotiate a link and, if the user opts in, to bring up a Thunderbolt Bridge network. No hub, switch, router, or hub configuration is required. The bridge operates at the data-link level, and macOS can, in certain configurations, expose the two machines to each other as peers, enabling file sharing through SMB or AFP, screen sharing, and, if desired, a zero-configuration local network over which both machines can reach shared resources.

The practical consequences were significant for creative professionals. A video editor could move a 4K or 8K timeline, a multi-terabyte music session, or a large machine-learning dataset between a desktop Mac Pro and a MacBook Pro at rates that effectively saturated the cable. Where an internal SATA SSD might deliver 500 megabytes per second and a 1 GbE port roughly 110 megabytes per second, a Thunderbolt 2 bridge approached the full 2.5 gigabytes per second that the 20 Gbps link allowed. For jobs that had previously consumed an evening, the transfer became a coffee break.

The feature also proved useful for diagnostics and recovery. A Thunderbolt bridge between two Macs offered a trusted path when Wi-Fi was unavailable and when the receiving Mac was booted into a sparse or single-user environment. Because the link did not depend on network services, it was among the few reliable ways to move files on to or off of a machine whose network stack was misbehaving.

Thunderbolt 2's direct-networking capability was quietly superseded as Thunderbolt 3 and USB-C arrived with symmetric 40 Gbps lanes and as macOS's network stack matured, but it established the template. It taught users that the same port that drives a display can also move a terabyte, and it set the expectation that future generations would only widen the gap between the cable and every slower network option left behind.

Thunderbolt is based on the Intel/AMD RocketLake and the PCI Express and DisplayPort transport layers, and the protocol exposes a point-to-point link that the operating system treats as a network interface. On macOS, connecting a Thunderbolt 2 port on one Mac to a Thunderbolt 2 port on another Mac causes the system to negotiate a link and, if the user opts in, to bring up a Thunderbolt Bridge network. No hub, switch, router, or hub configuration is required. The bridge operates at the data-link level, and macOS can, in certain configurations, expose the two machines to each other as peers, enabling file sharing through SMB or AFP, screen sharing, and, if desired, a zero-configuration local network over which both machines can reach shared resources.

The practical consequences were significant for creative professionals. A video editor could move a 4K or 8K timeline, a multi-terabyte music session, or a large machine-learning dataset between a desktop Mac Pro and a MacBook Pro at rates that effectively saturated the cable. Where an internal SATA SSD might deliver 500 megabytes per second and a 1 GbE port roughly 110 megabytes per second, a Thunderbolt 2 bridge approached the full 2.5 gigabytes per second that the 20 Gbps link allowed. For jobs that had previously consumed an evening, the transfer became a coffee break.

The feature also proved useful for diagnostics and recovery. A Thunderbolt bridge between two Macs offered a trusted path when Wi-Fi was unavailable and when the receiving Mac was booted into a sparse or single-user environment. Because the link did not depend on network services, it was among the few reliable ways to move files on to or off of a machine whose network stack was misbehaving.

Thunderbolt 2's direct-networking capability was quietly superseded as Thunderbolt 3 and USB-C arrived with symmetric 40 Gbps lanes and as macOS's network stack matured, but it established the template. It taught users that the same port that drives a display can also move a terabyte, and it set the expectation that future generations would only widen the gap between the cable and every slower network option left behind.

steps.text:
# Why GPUs Need Cooling

A graphics processing unit is, in the most literal sense, a small square of silicon that converts electrical energy into computation, and almost all of that electrical energy ultimately becomes heat. Modern GPUs are dense — a single high-end chip may contain tens of billions of transistors packed into a die a few square centimeters wide, and under load it can dissipate three hundred watts or more. That is comparable to an incandescent light bulb, except the heat is released in a concentrated area that must be carried away quickly or the chip overheats. The need for cooling is therefore not an engineering luxury; it is a physical necessity dictated by the limits of the semiconductor itself.

The first reason is thermal survival. Silicon has a maximum operating temperature, typically around one hundred degrees Celsius for the core, and exceeding it triggers protective behavior. The GPU will reduce its clock speed — a process called thermal throttling — to generate less heat, which directly reduces performance. Prolonged operation above the safe range can degrade the chip, weaken solder joints, or in extreme cases cause permanent damage. Cooling exists, in part, simply to keep the device inside the envelope its designers specified.

The second reason is that heat is a barrier to performance. A GPU boosts its clocks dynamically, raising frequencies as long as power and thermal headroom allow. If heat accumulates faster than it is removed, the boost ceiling drops and the card settles at a lower, sustained frequency. In other words, the quality of the cooling directly determines how much of the chip's rated performance a user actually gets. Two identical cards with different coolers can deliver measurably different frame rates for exactly this reason.

The third reason concerns the components around the die. A GPU is not a lone chip; it is surrounded by memory modules, voltage-regulator stages, and capacitors that all run hot. The memory in particular is sensitive to temperature, and sustained heat shortens component life and can cause instability. A good cooling solution manages the thermal load of the whole module, not just the central processor.

Finally, there are the quieter, everyday consequences: noise, longevity, and reliability. A card that runs hot must spin its fans faster to compensate, which raises noise. Sustained thermal cycling — repeated heating and cooling — stresses materials over years of use. Effective cooling keeps temperatures lower, fans quieter, and the card stable across its useful life.

Ultimately, GPUs need cooling because computation is thermodynamically expensive, and the only way to keep a densely packed, high-power chip performing at its designed speed is to move the resulting heat away faster than it is produced.
